title: The Language Check Can Stop Your Truck: ELP Out-of-Service Risk After the Comment Window
summary: English proficiency is already an out-of-service violation at roadside. Here is how carriers and brokers should protect cover, trip records, and DQ files now.
body_markdown:
## The load that stops at the inspection site


Picture a dry van load that picks up at a border-area warehouse before sunrise. It delivers to a distribution center several hundred miles inland the next morning. The appointment is tight, and the consignee charges for missed windows. A couple of hours into the run, the truck pulls into a roadside inspection. The inspector starts in English, has doubts, and moves to a structured interview. The driver can't answer basic questions about the trip in English and is placed out of service.


The equipment is fine and the paperwork is in order. The freight still sits until a qualified driver arrives. Every hour of that wait lands on someone: the carrier, the broker, the shipper, or the consignee who has to reschedule the dock.


This is no longer an edge case you brief once a year. FMCSA's August 2026 proposed rule cites federal enforcement data showing that English language proficiency (ELP) violations led to 19,045 out-of-service orders between June 25, 2025 and March 19, 2026. The comment window on writing that practice into the rules closed on October 9, 2026. For operations leaders, the question isn't how the final rule will read. It's whether your team can see which loads are exposed before dispatch, and who owns the recovery when one stops.


## What changed, in order


The requirement itself is old. Under 49 CFR 391.11(b)(2), a driver must read and speak English well enough to talk with the general public, understand highway traffic signs and signals in English, respond to official inquiries, and make entries on reports and records. The rule traces back to the Interstate Commerce Commission's Motor Carrier Safety Regulations, adopted December 23, 1936 and published January 22, 1937. The exceptions for drivers already in service were removed on May 27, 1939. What changed in 2025 and 2026 is the penalty for failing it.


### April 2025: the executive order


Executive Order 14286, "Enforcing Commonsense Rules of the Road for America's Truck Drivers," was issued April 28, 2025 and published at 90 FR 18759 on May 2, 2025. It told FMCSA to rescind its 2016 guidance, which had kept ELP violations from triggering out-of-service orders. It also told FMCSA to make sure the CVSA out-of-service criteria treat ELP violations as out of service.


### May and June 2025: out-of-service orders return at the roadside


On May 1, 2025, the CVSA Board voted to add 391.11(b)(2) to the North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria, effective June 25, 2025. FMCSA's May 20, 2025 policy memo (MC-SEE-2025-0001) rescinded the 2016 policy and set out the roadside process. The inspector starts in English. If there is doubt, a two-step assessment follows. The first step is a driver interview built around official inquiries. If the driver passes, the second step is a highway traffic sign recognition check that includes changeable message signs.


### April 2026: the border commercial zone line moves


FMCSA's April 16, 2026 policy memo (MC-SEE-2026-0002) replaced the May 2025 memo. It changed how inspectors treat drivers inside U.S. and Mexico border commercial zones. Before placing a driver out of service inside those zones, the inspector now works out the scope of the driver's current trip. They use the bill of lading, dispatch records, equipment interchange documents, driver statements, and shipping papers.


If the current trip would take the driver outside the zones, the driver goes out of service. If the current trip stays inside the zones, the driver is cited but not placed out of service for ELP. That holds even if the cargo later moves beyond the zone with a different driver. On April 19, 2026, CVSA updated its criteria to reference "current FMCSA enforcement guidance," which extended the April memo to State inspectors as well.


### August 2026: the proposed rule


On August 10, 2026, FMCSA published a notice of proposed rulemaking at 91 FR 51422 to 51431 (Docket FMCSA-2026-0826, RIN 2126-AC99, "English Language Proficiency; Out of Service Criteria"). It would amend 49 CFR 390.5, 390.5T, and 391.11 to make an ELP violation an out-of-service condition in the regulations. The commercial zone exception would move into a new 391.11(c). The proposal responds to a CVSA petition filed October 25, 2025.


### October 9, 2026: comments closed


Comments were due October 9, 2026. That ends the input phase, not the risk. Roadside enforcement already runs on the April 2026 guidance. The exposure exists today, whenever a final rule arrives.


## What the enforcement numbers say


The NPRM's own figures, drawn from federal inspection data, show how big the shift is. From January 1 to June 24, 2025, inspectors recorded 7,812 ELP violations and 33 out-of-service orders. From June 25, 2025 to March 19, 2026, they recorded 60,399 violations and 19,045 out-of-service orders, all outside border commercial zones. Violations inside the zones during that period were written as citations without out-of-service orders, under the practice in place at the time.


The proposal also puts a price on the narrower border exception. FMCSA estimates about 9,000 more out-of-service orders per year inside border commercial zones. It uses a downtime proxy of about $800 per day, over about two days to find a replacement driver. That works out to an estimated carrier cost of about $14.4 million a year. Treat the $800 figure as a regulatory proxy, not your number. Your real cost also includes reschedules, re-covers, and customer penalties.


## Trip documentation is now a cover asset


The April 2026 memo makes paperwork the deciding factor at the roadside. The commercial zones are defined in 49 CFR part 372, subpart B. Inside a zone, the inspector asks one narrow question: where is this driver's current trip going? The answer comes from the documents in the cab and the dispatch record behind them.


That creates a failure mode most shops have never had to plan for. A shipper's bill of lading often names a final consignee hundreds of miles inland, even when the plan is a short drayage move to a border yard and a swap to a different driver. If the paperwork in the cab reads like a through move, the driver can be treated as leaving the zone. If dispatch records, interchange documents, and the driver's own statement all show a move that ends at the yard inside the zone, the result can be a citation instead of a stranded load.


So the move structure has to be clear and consistent in every record an inspector might see. The drayage leg needs its own dispatch, destination, and interchange trail. The line-haul leg needs a separate driver assignment. This isn't about gaming the rule. It's about documents that describe what you're actually doing.


## Asset, broker, hybrid: who owns the failure


### Asset carriers


For an asset fleet, ELP sits squarely in the driver qualification (DQ) file. The carrier hires, qualifies, and dispatches the driver, so the carrier owns the out-of-service order, the inspection record, and the safety exposure. ELP out-of-service orders go into the same inspection history that shapes how enforcement and customers see your fleet.


The practical decision is whether ELP becomes a documented check at onboarding and at set intervals, applied consistently and fairly, or stays a road test supervisor's judgment call. It also means knowing ahead of time which drivers you can send to relieve a stranded truck, and how fast.


### Brokers


A broker doesn't own the DQ file, but it owns the promise to the customer. When a contracted carrier's driver goes out of service mid-lane, the broker is the one re-covering the load, explaining, and absorbing the service failure. The decision is how much carrier vetting to build around ELP risk without crossing into controlling the carrier's drivers.


Reasonable steps include:


-


Adding roadside ELP history to carrier review.


-


Asking carriers on border lanes how they structure zone moves.


-


Requiring trip documents that clearly separate the zone leg from the line-haul leg when the broker builds the tender.


### Hybrids


Hybrids face both problems at once, often on the same lane. The useful decision is which loads go to company drivers and which go to brokered capacity when a lane crosses a commercial zone boundary. A border transload that hands off to a company driver at the yard may carry less risk than a single through move on a brokered carrier you can't see into. Hybrids also need billing that puts recovery costs on the right business unit.


## Where workflow design earns its keep


Every freight operation runs these lanes differently. A cross-border specialist with its own drayage, an inland fleet that rarely sees the border, and a brokerage with a deep carrier base each need different rules. Generic setups treat a driver as qualified or not, and a load as covered or not. The systems that hold up under ELP enforcement are set up to match how each business actually moves freight.


A few patterns are worth building into dispatch and carrier management:


-


**ELP and DQ status flags.** Record ELP checks as part of driver qualification, with a review date. Dispatch then sees the status before assignment, not after an inspection.


-


**Hold rules when dock communication fails.** If a shipper or receiver reports that a driver couldn't communicate at the dock, send that to a review status instead of leaving it as an informal note.


-


**Zone-aware lane rules.** Tag each lane as inside a border commercial zone, crossing out of one, or fully inland. Require split legs and separate driver assignments where the move structure depends on it.


-


**Two-source trip scope checks.** Confirm that the dispatch record and the documents in the cab describe the same current trip. A mismatch between the BOL destination and a dispatch that stays inside the zone is exactly the gap an inspector will look at.


-


**Out-of-service evidence packets.** When a load is stranded, gather the inspection report, timestamps, communications, replacement driver dispatch, and detention or reschedule charges in one place. That packet supports claims, customer credits, and carrier scorecards later.


-


**Permissions and escalation.** Decide who can release a load after an ELP stop, who tells the customer, and who approves recovery spend. Build it into the system so the answer doesn't depend on who is on shift.


None of this needs a new department. It needs workflows that match your network, not someone else's template.


## A related deadline has already passed


ELP isn't the only qualification-related trigger on the road right now. On August 6, 2026, FMCSA removed five devices from its list of registered ELDs, and carriers had until October 6, 2026 to replace them. After that date, using a revoked device counts as operating without an ELD. That means a citation under 395.8(a)(1) and an out-of-service order. If any part of your fleet or carrier base was on one of those devices, confirm the replacement today.


## What to run this week


The comment window is closed, and enforcement isn't waiting. A short list for this week:


1.


Pull every ELP violation and out-of-service order on your fleet or carrier base since June 25, 2025. Find the lanes and terminals where they cluster.


2.


Map your border commercial zone lanes. Mark which moves stay inside the zones and which leave them.


3.


Audit one week of border loads to check that the BOL, dispatch record, interchange documents, and driver assignment all match.


4.


Confirm your ELP qualification practice is documented, applied consistently, and recorded in the DQ file. Include drivers with FMCSA hearing exemptions under 391.41(b)(11). They aren't unqualified under ELP if they can read and write English (per FMCSA guidance at 79 FR 59139, October 1, 2014).


5.


Build a stranded-load playbook: relief driver options by region, customer notification templates, and a named owner for recovery costs.


6.


For brokers, add ELP roadside history and zone-move structure to carrier review on border lanes.


7.


Verify that no truck in your network is still running a revoked ELD after the October 6, 2026 deadline.


8.


Read the NPRM text in Docket FMCSA-2026-0826 so your team can adjust quickly when FMCSA acts on it.


The language check takes a few minutes at the roadside. The recovery can take two days. The operations that keep freight moving will treat ELP like any other qualification gate and build their workflows to see it coming.


## FAQ


### Is an English language proficiency violation an out-of-service condition today?


Yes. CVSA added 49 CFR 391.11(b)(2) to the North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria effective June 25, 2025, and roadside enforcement now follows FMCSA's April 16, 2026 guidance. A driver who fails the ELP assessment can be placed out of service now, before any final rule, unless the border commercial zone exception applies.


### What did the August 10, 2026 proposed rule do?


It proposed making ELP violations an out-of-service condition in the federal regulations. The NPRM (91 FR 51422, Docket FMCSA-2026-0826, RIN 2126-AC99) would amend 49 CFR 390.5, 390.5T, and 391.11 and add the commercial zone exception as a new 391.11(c). Comments closed October 9, 2026.


### How does the border commercial zone exception work now?


It depends on the driver's current trip. Under the April 16, 2026 memo, inspectors use the bill of lading, dispatch records, interchange documents, driver statements, and shipping papers to decide whether the current trip leaves the zone. If it does, the driver goes out of service. If it stays inside, the driver is cited but not placed out of service for ELP.


### How does a roadside ELP assessment work?


The inspector starts in English and, if in doubt, runs a two-step check. The first step is a driver interview built around official inquiries. If the driver passes, the second step is highway traffic sign recognition, including changeable message signs.


### Does a broker carry ELP risk if it does not employ the driver?


Yes, in practice. The carrier owns the driver qualification file and the out-of-service record. The broker owns the customer commitment and the re-cover when a contracted driver is stopped mid-lane, so carrier review and clear trip documents on border lanes matter to brokers too.


### What does an ELP out-of-service order cost?


FMCSA's proposal uses a proxy of about $800 per day of downtime over roughly two days to replace a driver. That figure supports its estimate of about $14.4 million a year in carrier cost from roughly 9,000 additional border-zone out-of-service orders. Your actual cost will also include reschedules, re-covers, and customer penalties.
